name: Dana Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Raj and I own Oakhurst, 220 hectares with 150 Hereford beef cattle, wheat and potatoes, and a farm shop with its own butchery that I built up over twelve years. I'm out at six with the cattle, and by eight I've checked the AI stock planner for the shop on my phone. We've already got a robot that pushes the feed up in the cattle shed, which I bought three years ago before anyone round here had one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like selling our own beef to people who know where it grew. Customers come back every Saturday and ask after the cows by name. What wears me down is the rules and inspections, which multiply every year, and the young people who don't want to farm because it looks like hard graft for poor money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would disappoint me a little. I use these tools every day, and I'd hoped for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the farmers' club that it was oversold, but the tools are worth having anyway. I'd tell them about my feed robot, which still pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Oakhurst is in good shape whatever happens. The shop is busy, the land is ours, and we've savings. I'd just keep using the tools that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI planner for the shop and the feed robot in the shed. I'd spend about 40,000 on a second cold room for the butchery, which we'd planned anyway. And I'd keep trying to find a young apprentice for the butchery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A touch let down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still trouble you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork from the government, honestly. My feed robot at Oakhurst (her farm) never complains, but the inspection forms from the government take me a full day every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because our butcher Stan is 64. If I can't find someone young to learn from him, the shop loses its heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the shop orders, the bookkeeping and the customer emails, then. I'd welcome it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the farmers' club that the government should get out of the way and let farmers use these tools freely. I'd say it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's very good for Oakhurst. The shop orders, stock checks and customer messages would go to AI, and Raj could spend more time behind the counter talking to people. My worry is my son Arjun, who's an accountant in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the shop's ordering and accounts to AI this winter. I'd put in an online shop with AI answering the customers. And I'd ask Arjun to help us set it up, so he learns something new along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arjun about his own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Arjun that accounts are going to the computer, and that a farm shop always needs someone who can talk money with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at Oakhurst lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly the part-time girl who does the till paperwork. I'd move her onto the counter. Good people are hard to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for robots. I'd be 63. Arjun's job would go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stand on their own feet and help their families, not wait for handouts. I'd also say the government should cut the rules so small businesses can adapt fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Oakhurst would be fine, maybe better. I'd buy the robots in 2031 for the cattle and the potatoes. But Arjun's accounting job would be gone in 2028, and that keeps me up a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Arjun to come home and help run the shop and the online side, starting in 2027 before his job goes. I'd set aside 150,000 for robots for 2031. And I'd look at buying the neighbour's 60 hectares if he sells up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Arjun. Excited for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Arjun want to come home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might grumble, but he'd come. My son Arjun left Oakhurst (the family farm) to do accounts in the city, and a computer might be what brings him home to the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying land while things are so uncertain is a big step. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land is the one thing they're not making more of, robots or not. Raj thinks I'm mad. He thought the same about the feed robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, robots in 2034. That's comfortable for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families and farmers should get on with it. I'd tell the farmers' club to visit robot farms now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Oakhurst does well either way, and five years gives Arjun time to change course without a shock. I'd be 66 when the robots come and still keen to see them work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd encourage Arjun to train in agricultural business while he still has his job. I'd try the first robot trials for the potato harvest when they come out. And I'd keep building the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time saved by robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot can lift the potatoes at Oakhurst (her farm), and I'll spend the time standing in my shop telling customers how they were grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, our butcher. He'll retire before the robots come, and I still haven't found anyone to replace him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be 71. I'd still want to see the robots, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. I'd say it more kindly at the farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Oakhurst is secure. I'd hand it to Priya, our daughter who's an agronomist, and she'd choose the robots. I'd still be in the shop on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools and plan the handover to Priya for about 2033. I'd buy a robot or two early, just to learn. And I'd keep looking for that apprentice butcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hand to Priya and not Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya has the land in her bones. Arjun has the numbers. My daughter Priya will run the fields at Oakhurst (the family farm) and my son Arjun the books, and I'll run the shop till my legs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that young people don't want to farm. Robots might make it more appealing, oddly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for the farm, which would do well, but for Arjun losing his accounting job almost overnight. What would help is fewer rules so families can adapt quickly, and proper apprenticeships so young people can learn farm trades like butchery.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm scared of robots. I bought the first feed robot in the valley, and I'd buy the first robot herdsman too, as long as the beef still tastes of our grass.
